new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is contrastive (phonemic) and must be listed per word: in the disyllabic minimal pairs it falls on either the first (penultimate) or the last syllable with no segmental cue, and the 2000 dictionary (Gelacio, Loong & Schumacher, sect. 1.3) therefore marks stress on every headword with an apostrophe before the stressed syllable, describing the stressed syllable as 'usually a longer syllable with a slightly louder volume' ('hilu 'thread' vs hi'lu 'poison'). In the dictionary's example tables stress sits on the penult or the ultima, never earlier, in 2-3 syllable words (a'baga, ri'pulyu vs dadu'wa, wo'hig). No source gives a rule predicting the position.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any source examined.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Weaver & Weaver 1963 (p.3) explicitly deferred stress ('has not been completely analyzed'); no later source retracts the phonemic-stress claim. Note the contrast with Zorc 1978's general remark (held under ilia1236) that Manobo languages 'have lost contrastive accent' -- for Agusan Manobo the two first-hand sources say the opposite.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms in isolation (minimal pairs; dictionary headwords). Phonetic correlates per the 2000 dictionary: duration plus slight loudness. 1978 data from Kasapa Dos, La Paz, Agusan del Sur (seven months' fieldwork); Umayam vs Adgawan dialects distinguished only for the /j/ phoneme. The dictionary covers the Agusan river valley and the eastern Diwata range.
new_statements.identity_note: Language-level agus1235 (ISO msm). Schumacher & Schumacher 1978 data are from Kasapa Dos, La Paz, Agusan del Sur and they name the Umayam and Adgawan dialects (Glottolog dialects umay1237, adga1237); Weaver & Weaver 1963 worked in Sagunto, La Paz, Agusan; the 2000 dictionary covers the Agusan river valley and the eastern Diwata range. Elkins 1974 (p.635) subsumes Agusan Manobo under Dibabawon (DIB, ISO mbd) as dialects, so Dibabawon descriptions (e.g. Forster & Barnard 1987 'high pitch.. on the penultimate syllable of a normal statement', held under atam1240) concern a closely related but separately coded variety, not this one.

sources.note: Sect. 1.3 'Stress' (PDF p.6 of 10, front matter unpaginated): 'Stress in Manobo words is usually a longer syllable with a slightly louder volume. Stress is very important in Manobo in telling words apart. Therefore, stress is written in this dictionary. We write it with an apostrophe (') before the stressed syllable. For example, the only difference between 'hilu 'thread' and hi'lu 'poison', is stress. In the first word, the first syllable is stressed. In the second word, the second syllable is stressed.'
